title: Halcyon Bioinformatics POC - Tail Latency Mitigation & Resilience Report
body:
Executive summary:

This document captures the benchmarking we ran for the Halcyon Bioinformatics proof-of-concept (POC) focused on sequence-annotation queries characteristic of a research pipeline. Primary objective: identify the drivers of tail latency (p95/p99/p999) under mixed short/long sequence workloads and produce concrete mitigation recommendations that balance cost and end-user experience.

High-level result: by combining small-window prefix caching, adaptive micro-batching with a 60ms max-wait threshold, and a conservative 4-bit quantized model variant for background (non-critical) paths, we reduced p99 tail latency for the critical endpoint from ~1.8s baseline down to ~420ms while increasing sustained throughput by 2.1x and keeping incremental cost < 35% relative to baseline. Hedged requests for extreme outliers (p999) gave an additional 30-40% reduction at a modest cost and complexity tradeoff.

Scope and goals:
- Workload: Sequence annotation queries submitted from Halcyon’s research UI; mixture of short (<=128 tokens), medium (129-1024 tokens), and long (>=1025 tokens) sequences. 70/20/10 split respectively.
- Metrics: latency distribution (p50/p95/p99/p999), throughput (qps), GPU utilization, token cost (normalized $/1k tokens), and error/retry rates.
- Constraints: interactive user-facing SLO = p95 < 500ms for short/medium queries; allow longer for long sequences but aim for p99 < 1.5s where possible. Budget target: < 35% uplift vs existing CPU-based baseline for the same QPS.

Test environment:
- Platform: Redwood Dedicated (staging cluster) with isolated GPU pool (A100 80GB equiv) and autoscaler disabled for consistency.
- Models tested:
  * redwood-chat-16k-v1 (fp16 baseline)
  * redwood-chat-16k-v1-4bit (quantized 4-bit variant)
  * open-llama-13b-quant (4-bit, optimized kernels)
- Serving runtime: Redwood inference runtime v1.9.2 (kernel selection enabled, KV cache warmup hooks on).
- Network: single-region (us-west-2) with <1ms intra-cluster latency.
- Load generator: custom concourse harness modeled on Halcyon client behavior (think time, jitter, and occasional burst submissions).

Workload details and realism:
- Realistic user patterns: 15% of short requests contained structured tool calls (function-calling style prompts) which exercise the runtime’s structured output path.
- Long queries simulate large reference alignments (mean token length ~1800 tokens). These dominate compute but are rare (10%).
- Burst pattern: 100 users simultaneously submitting short queries for interactive exploration (spike scenario).

Test matrix (representative runs):
- Baseline: redwood-chat-16k-v1 fp16, stock batching (max 128), no prefix caching, cold kv cache.
- Caching + adaptive batching: same model, enabled prefix caching for repeated prefixes (common for Halcyon), micro-batch max-wait 60ms, dynamic max batch size tuned to 32 for short sequences.
- Quantized variant: redwood-chat-16k-v1-4bit with same batching/caching config.
- Hedged requests: adaptive policy sending second replica after 250ms if no token output for critical short queries.
- Long-query backgrounding: route long queries to dedicated nodes with higher batch sizes and lower preemption priority.

Key numeric results (aggregated):
- Baseline (fp16, no-cache): short p95 = 720ms, p99 = 1.82s, p999 = 4.6s; throughput 240 qps sustained; cost baseline $0.95 / 1k tokens (normalized).
- Caching + adaptive batching (fp16): short p95 = 360ms, p99 = 820ms, p999 = 2.1s; throughput 380 qps; cost change +12%.
- Quantized (4-bit) + caching + adaptive batching: short p95 = 290ms, p99 = 420ms, p999 = 1.3s; throughput 510 qps; cost change +28% (quantization reduced GPU time but increased tokenization overhead marginally).
- Hedged requests on top of quantized config (hedge timeout 250ms): p999 reduced to ~820ms (from 1.3s) for critical short queries; 1.1x overall cost multiplier for hedged path (only applies to ~15% critical calls).
- Long-query path (dedicated nodes): long p95 = 5.4s, p99 = 9.8s (acceptable for batch-style long jobs); segregation prevented long-job interference on short-query tail.

Observations and root causes for tail latency:
1) Cold KV cache and first-token generation variability: long-tail spikes often traced to requests that lacked warm KV caches (prefixless queries or new user sessions). Warmup during concurrent requests produced queuing and kernel selection stalls.
2) Large sequence interference: long queries with large batch size caused memory pressure and occasional kernel re-selection, injecting 100-300ms stalls affecting co-located short requests when sharing nodes.
3) Scheduling jitter: stock global batching produced some large batches with long queue-wait times when bursty arrivals occurred, amplifying p99.
4) OS-level preemption and CUDA context switches: occasional outliers correlated with background maintenance jobs on the host (we replicated by running noisy housekeeping and seeing same pattern).

Mitigation strategies evaluated:
- Prefix/KV caching: enabling request-level prefix caching reduced first-token cost for repeated patterns (Halcyon’s UI issues many similar prompts) and reduced variance significantly. Cache invalidation was tuned to 5m for interactive flows.
- Adaptive micro-batching: enforce max-wait thresholds (we used 60ms) so short queries are not held for long batch formation; lower threshold decreases throughput but improves tail.
- Dedicated long-query nodes: route >=1025 token requests to separate pool with larger batch sizes and lower preemption. Prevented head-of-line blocking for short queries.
- Quantized model variants: 4-bit quantization gave good latency/throughput wins; for critical fidelity paths we suggest A/B tests on held-out prompts to measure any downstream quality impact.
- Hedged requests: used selectively for critical short interactions, sending duplicate to second replica after 250ms; effective for p999 but increases cost and complexity (idempotency/duplicate suppression needed).

Recommended production configuration for Halcyon POC:
1) Default route (interactive UI): redwood-chat-16k-v1-4bit with prefix caching enabled, adaptive micro-batching (max-wait 60ms, max-batch 32 for short requests). Can be deployed on a single Dedicated pool with 3 nodes per 1000 concurrent interactive users.
2) Critical path hedging: enable hedged requests only for the top-10% highest-SLA endpoints (function calls, tool triggers). Hedge timeout 250ms; track duplicate-suppression metrics.
3) Long-job pool: separate Dedicated nodes sized for throughput (batch size 128), quantized models allowed, background priority.
4) Observability: add per-request cache-hit flag, kernel-version tag, and queue-wait time to Redwood Console dashboards. Create alert if p95 > 500ms or cache-hit < 40% for interactive flows.

Cost estimate (rough):
- Baseline monthly infra (simulated steady-state at target QPS): $11k
- Recommended config (with quantized + minor capacity increase + hedged for critical 15%): ~$14k (approx +27%), within Halcyon budget threshold (<35%).

Runbook excerpt (for on-call):
- Symptom A: p95 for interactive UI > 600ms
  * Check cache-hit rate in console (metric: request.cache_hit). If < 30% -> consider rolling prefix cache warm-up job or extend cache TTL.
  * Check queue-wait time histograms; if many requests hitting >60ms wait, temporarily increase instance count by 1 in dedicated pool.
- Symptom B: sudden p999 spikes for short requests
  * Check recent hedged request success rate (metric: hedge.success_ratio). If hedges are being dropped, inspect duplicate suppression logs.
  * Look for kernel switch events in runtime logs; correlate with model variant updates.

Open questions and follow-ups with Halcyon engineering:
- Tolerance for quantization: run human-in-the-loop fidelity evaluation on a Halcyon-curated set of 400 prompts to validate 4-bit variant for labelling correctness.
- Security/compliance: long-term plan for encrypted model artifacts on private deployment if Halcyon requests on-prem.
- Autoscaling policy: confirm target SLOs under autoscaler events and whether faster scale-up is acceptable vs overprovisioning.

Appendix: notable logs and reproductions (summary)
- Repro case A (cold start event): 2027-02-10 15:12 UTC — 90% of p999 outliers correlated with new session traffic; reproducer script provided in linked github PR.
- Repro case B (noisy host): simulated housekeeping process increased host-level RT by ~120ms for small fraction of requests; recommendation: pin inference nodes away from scheduled housekeeping windows or isolate with node taints.

Next steps (recommended):
- Schedule a 2-week fidelity trial of redwood-chat-16k-v1-4bit with Halcyon labellers (metric: label agreement >95% threshold).
- Implement hedged requests behind a feature flag for the top-10% critical endpoints; monitor cost and p999 over a 7-day window.
- Deliver a minimal ops playbook for cache warm-ups and node isolation to Halcyon SRE team.

Contact and ownership:
- SE lead: Priya Menon (pri@redwood.ai)
- Solutions support: Diego Alvarez (diego@redwood.ai), Maya Chen (maya@redwood.ai)

Notes: this is an intentionally scoped POC report — results are representative of our staging dedicated environment and should be validated on Halcyon’s own private deployment before committing to production SLAs.
